picks.excerpt: AI dominated keynotes, panels, and even opening remarks at the 35th International Publishers Association Congress in Kuala Lumpur (July 5-9, ~500 participants from 40 countries). Keynote speaker Thad McIlroy said publishing has moved past the 'golly-gee-whiz phase of AI' to the 'what the heck am I going to do about it?' phase, while IPA president Gvantsa Jobava called publishers' collective work 'the best source of training data for AI.'
picks.rationale: AI dominating the agenda of global publishing's flagship congress (500 participants, 40 countries) is the week's clearest industry signal; kept over the Publishing Perspectives piece on the same event (one story family — PW's angle is more AI-substantive).

picks.excerpt: Publishers are still waiting for 'clear' legal answers on AI training, outputs, and licensing, the Publishers' Licensing Services Conference heard — years of copyright litigation have yet to resolve the key questions publishers need answered before committing to AI licensing strategies.
picks.rationale: Actionable legal-landscape check: litigation still hasn't answered the training/output/licensing questions publishers need — a distinct angle from the already-published 07-07 PLS collective-licensing opt-in card.

picks.excerpt: Bryan Charles traces AI's slow, steady invasion of literary translation through the test case of translating Proust with ChatGPT, talking with translators Andrew Rothwell and Sam Taylor about how AI tools have reduced the 'cognitive load' of literary translation — and what is lost when they do.
picks.rationale: Freshest item in the pool (07-07) and a concrete craft-level test of AI in literary translation, with working translators weighing what reduced 'cognitive load' gains and loses.

picks.excerpt: Cambridge University Press, COUNTER, and NISO convened nearly three dozen experts — libraries, AI tool developers, funders, publishers, platforms — to build frameworks that make AI use of scholarly content traceable and measurable: usage metrics, provenance, and attribution standards for generative AI systems.
picks.rationale: Concrete standards work (CUP/COUNTER/NISO on provenance and usage metrics for AI use of scholarly content) that publishers can plug into — distinct from previously published Scholarly Kitchen cards.

picks.excerpt: Friedman highlights new research analyzing 500,000 anonymized ChatGPT conversations that identifies 'infinite story demanders' — a small cohort of power users generating large volumes of repetitive AI fanfiction and erotica for personal consumption — evidence that LLMs enable interactive, playful, permutating story consumption outside traditional publishing.
picks.rationale: Deprioritized to last slot: its lead research overlaps the 07-06 games card (PC Gamer angle), but cross-section is not a hard block, the fresh books pool is exhausted, and Friedman's publishing-side reading (story consumption migrating outside traditional publishing) is a distinct angle.

dropped_as_published_duplicate.reason: Follow-up duplicate of the Granta/Commonwealth AI-accusation card published 2026-06-29 in this section; the win-after-clearing angle was already judged a duplicate in yesterday's curation and the article adds nothing substantially new.

dropped_within_pool.reason: Same story family as the Publishers Weekly IPA Congress pick (35th IPA Congress, Kuala Lumpur); kept the stronger, more AI-focused PW article.
